content: This report provides an updated summary of recommendations for vaccinating healthcare personnel (HCP) in the United States, as previously outlined by the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) and the Healthcare Infection Control Practices Advisory Committee (HICPAC). The updated recommendations aim to assist hospital administrators, infection control practitioners, employee health clinicians, and HCP in optimizing infection prevention and control programs. These recommendations are categorized by disease into two groups: (1) diseases for which vaccination or documentation of immunity is recommended due to occupational risks of acquiring or transmitting the disease, and (2) diseases for which vaccination may be indicated under specific circumstances. The report includes background information on each vaccine-preventable disease, specific recommendations for vaccine use, and infection control measures related to vaccination. It also summarizes ACIP recommendations for other vaccines recommended for adults, considerations for catch-up and travel vaccinations, and work restrictions. Healthcare personnel are defined as all paid and unpaid individuals working in healthcare settings who may be exposed to patients or infectious materials, including body substances, contaminated medical supplies, equipment, environmental surfaces, or air. This includes not only those directly involved in patient care but also individuals in roles such as clerical, dietary, housekeeping, and maintenance, who may be exposed to infectious agents. Due to their contact with patients or infectious materials, many HCP are at risk of exposure to and potential transmission of vaccine-preventable diseases. Employers are encouraged to maintain vaccination records for HCP, including documentation of disease history, vaccination history, serology results, and any adverse events following vaccination. These records should include details such as the date of vaccine administration, vaccine manufacturer, lot number, and the name and title of the person administering the vaccine. HCP should be provided with a copy of their vaccination records and encouraged to keep them with their personal health records for future reference. HICPAC recommends that facilities providing direct patient care establish comprehensive vaccination policies for all HCP. The American Hospital Association has endorsed vaccination programs for both hospital personnel and patients. The recommendations emphasize the importance of routine vaccination for diseases such as hepatitis B, influenza, measles, mumps, rubella, pertussis, and varicella, as these diseases pose significant risks of nosocomial transmission. Vaccination for other diseases, such as meningococcal disease, typhoid, and polio, may be indicated in specific circumstances. Hepatitis B vaccination is particularly critical for HCP due to the high risk of occupational exposure to blood and body fluids. The virus is highly infectious, and transmission from a needlestick injury involving hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg)-positive blood is significantly more likely than transmission of HIV. The hepatitis B vaccine has been shown to be highly effective, with a three-dose series inducing protective antibody levels in the majority of healthy adults. Immunity has been documented to persist for over 22 years in vaccine responders. Influenza vaccination is recommended annually for all HCP, not just those with direct patient care duties. Influenza can cause significant morbidity and mortality, particularly among vulnerable populations such as the elderly, young children, and individuals with chronic medical conditions. Vaccination of HCP reduces the risk of occupationally acquired influenza and transmission to patients. Comprehensive programs to increase vaccine coverage among HCP are needed, and vaccination rates within facilities should be regularly measured and reported. For measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR), a history of disease is no longer considered adequate evidence of immunity for HCP. Laboratory confirmation of disease or vaccination history is required. Pertussis vaccination with Tdap is recommended for all HCP, regardless of age, with no minimum interval required since the last tetanus or diphtheria-containing vaccine. Varicella immunity criteria for HCP include written documentation of two doses of vaccine, laboratory evidence of immunity or disease confirmation, or a diagnosis of varicella or herpes zoster by a healthcare provider. Meningococcal vaccination is recommended for HCP with specific medical conditions, such as asplenia or complement deficiencies, and for those with HIV infection. Postexposure prophylaxis for hepatitis B should be evaluated immediately after potential exposure to blood or body fluids. Decisions should be based on the HBsAg status of the source and the vaccination and immune status of the exposed HCP. Hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) and the hepatitis B vaccine should be administered as soon as possible after exposure, preferably within 24 hours. Influenza vaccination programs should address barriers to vaccine acceptance among HCP, such as concerns about side effects, perceived vaccine ineffectiveness, and fear of needles. Strategies to increase vaccine uptake include providing vaccines at no cost, offering them at convenient locations and times, and educating HCP about the benefits of vaccination. Facilities should develop comprehensive influenza vaccination strategies, including targeted education and accessible vaccination sites. The safety of vaccines, including hepatitis B and influenza vaccines, has been well-documented. Adverse events are rare, and vaccination is contraindicated only for individuals with a history of severe allergic reactions to vaccine components. Pregnant women can safely receive the hepatitis B vaccine, as it poses no risk to the fetus. In summary, these updated recommendations provide a framework for protecting HCP and their patients from vaccine-preventable diseases through comprehensive vaccination policies and programs.
